summary: For 6-7 year-olds, strategic tool choice shifts from concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS (number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model), and the skill becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. The central proposed activity gives a child the same chooser facing two problems — a two-digit addition (34+28) where a number line's tens-and-ones jumps are genuinely quicker than counting a cube pile, and a measuring task where a ruler (or a metre stick for a large object), not a number line, fits — then invites them to justify why each tool fits its problem. Alternatives (a convince-a-partner dialogue, a primer comparison board) are intended to serve different pedagogical purposes.
misconceptions: Persists with counting single cubes in ones for two-digit numbers (34+28), which is slow and error-prone (EEF: over-reliance on concrete)
Mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose — e.g. reaches for a number line for a 'how long is it?' measuring task instead of a ruler
Draws a number line but counts every mark in ones anyway, using it as a ritual rather than to jump in tens (EEF: answer, not structure)
Thinks a representation is 'babyish' or 'proper' rather than fit-for-purpose, so choice is about status not the problem

activities.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
steps: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
activities.insight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.

activities.title: Convince a partner who defaults to cubes
steps: Work with a partner (or in-role character) who always reaches for cubes, even for 34 + 28.
Argue why a number line or hundred square is more efficient for big numbers — point to jumping the tens and avoiding miscounts.
Concede honestly where cubes still win: give a problem (e.g. a small total like 3 + 4) where cubes really would be the best choice.
Answer a probe such as 'What can a hundred square show you that a number line doesn't when you add 28?'
activities.insight: Being able to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem — and when the rejected tool would in fact be right — is what separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.

activities.title: Primer: what each tool is for
steps: Explore a comparison board for number line vs hundred square vs ruler, revealing 'best for…' and 'not for…' notes for each.
Before the main task, predict which tool you would reach for in an addition and in a measuring problem.
activities.insight: Each representation has a purpose and a limitation — a number line jumps along a count but does not measure a real object; cubes become unwieldy past twenty — so a warm-up can prime 'what each is for'.

checkQuestion: To work out 34 + 28, one child got out 62 cubes and counted them one by one; another used a number line and jumped +20 then +8. Which was the better tool for these numbers, and why? And when WOULD cubes be the better choice?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that counting single cubes for numbers this big is slow and error-prone (a limitation), that the number line lets you jump in tens and ones (efficiency and structure), AND that cubes are fine for small numbers — a fit judgement, not 'cubes are babyish'.
